recall.answer: No. It tests your judgment about numbers, not numbers you memorize.

sections.title: 1. First, understand the requirements. Then, design any GenAI application.

keyTerms.definition: Requirements that show what the system does, such as answering questions from documents.
Requirements that show how well the system does it, such as latency, scale, and cost.
Tokens per day equals requests per day times tokens per request, converting traffic into cost.
The correct answer to every system design question: it meets all limits and nothing costs less.

recall.question: What is the correct answer to every system design question?
recall.answer: The cheapest architecture that meets all limits.

recall.question: What does the token estimation equation compute?
recall.answer: Tokens per day equals requests per day times tokens per request, and the monthly bill multiplies by 30 days and price per token.

keyTerms.definition: One of the four ways to call a model, each with different latency, payload, and cost.
The request and response size each invocation pattern can carry.

recall.question: What does the exam test about invocation patterns?
recall.answer: The decision between patterns, not the API syntax.

The raw provider API needed for embeddings and provider-specific features.
A constraint like streaming that outranks a preference like cost when they conflict.

recall.answer: For embeddings and provider-specific features; Converse is for unified multi-provider code.

recall.question: What wins when a hard requirement conflicts with a preference?
recall.answer: The hard requirement; streaming to the browser beats wanting the cheapest option.

sections.title: 2.2 The decision ladder: latency, payload, use case

keyTerms.definition: The 29-second limit on API Gateway integrations that decides sync versus async.
Where long tasks like agent loops go instead of behind API Gateway.

recall.question: Why can a 3-minute agent loop not run behind API Gateway?
recall.answer: It exceeds the 29-second integration timeout, so put it in a queue.

keyTerms.definition: The sequence of hop limits where the smallest limit wins.
Retrying with growing waits plus jitter for throttling and temporary 5xx errors.
Stopping calls after repeated failures for a cool-down, saving tokens on doomed retries.

recall.question: What is the timeout chain rule?
recall.answer: Each hop has a limit and the smallest limit wins.

recall.question: When do you not retry?
recall.answer: On a bad request like a validation error; retry only throttling and temporary 5xx errors.

sections.title: 3. RAG on Bedrock: Knowledge Bases end to end

keyTerms.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation, grounding a model in your data instead of retraining it.
Showing the exact source section each answer came from, required when answers must be traceable.

recall.question: Which scenario words point to RAG?
recall.answer: Private documents, must cite sources, or answers grounded in company data.

keyTerms.definition: The managed RAG service that does ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing, and retrieval.
The one-call API where Bedrock generates the answer with citations.
The API that returns chunks only, leaving the prompt and model call to you.
The offline pipeline that parses documents into a data source on a sync schedule.

recall.question: When do you use Retrieve instead of RetrieveAndGenerate?
recall.answer: When you need custom prompt control, inline guardrails, or streaming.

recall.question: What are the two KB pipelines the exam tests?
recall.answer: Ingestion, which is offline on a sync schedule, and retrieval at query time.

keyTerms.definition: Where the KB gets documents, such as S3, a web crawler, Confluence, SharePoint, or Salesforce.
The hourly, daily, weekly, or on-demand cadence on which the KB re-ingests documents.
What retrieval actually searches; it only knows what the last sync ingested.

recall.question: Why are answers old after a document update?
recall.answer: Retrieval searches the vector index, which only knows the last sync; the KB does not read S3 live.

recall.question: Can you change chunking on an existing data source?
recall.answer: No. You must create the data source again.

keyTerms.definition: Dividing documents into retrievable units; the most important retrieval control.
Splitting on token count with overlap; simple but can split ideas across chunks.
Splitting at meaning boundaries; costs more compute at ingestion.
Linking child chunks to larger parent chunks that are injected as context.

recall.question: What fixes tables broken across chunks with answers missing row context?
recall.answer: Hierarchical chunking with advanced parsing.

recall.question: What is the debug order for bad RAG answers?
recall.answer: Chunking first, then embeddings, then the generation model last.

keyTerms.definition: The model that turns chunks and questions into vectors; Titan Text Embeddings v2 is the default.
The vector size setting, such as 1024, 512, or 256, trading storage and latency for quality.
Where vectors from different embeddings models live; they cannot be compared across models.

recall.question: Why can you not swap the embeddings model later?
recall.answer: Vectors from different models live in different spaces, so you must re-embed every chunk.

recall.question: Why is RAG cheap to operate per question?
recall.answer: The query side embeds only the question; the expensive embedding happens once at ingestion.

keyTerms.definition: The database that holds vectors and runs nearest-neighbor search, chosen once at KB creation.
The managed vector store option with built-in hybrid search.
Separate KBs with IAM-enforced isolation per tenant; Guardrails cannot do this.

recall.question: Why are DynamoDB and ElastiCache wrong as vector stores?
recall.answer: DynamoDB holds metadata and session state, not vectors; ElastiCache is ephemeral and for caching.

recall.question: How do you isolate tenants?
recall.answer: With separate KBs and IAM-enforced isolation per tenant.

keyTerms.definition: The number of chunks returned per query; a small k is cheap and specific.
Keyword plus vector search combined for better retrieval.
Re-scoring top chunks with a stronger model for relevance.

recall.question: What is the debug order for bad RAG answers?
recall.answer: Check retrieval, then relevance, and never start by changing the generation model.

keyTerms.definition: Retrieve for chunks, build the prompt yourself, then call the model through Converse.
The inline guardrail configuration on a Converse call for input and output screening.
Guardrails on inputs that stop injection and PII.

recall.question: Where do Guardrails fit in the manual RAG loop?
recall.answer: On inputs, outputs, or both per call; in RAG almost always both.

recall.question: When do you use Retrieve plus Converse instead of RetrieveAndGenerate?
recall.answer: When you need custom prompt control, inline guardrails, or streaming.

keyTerms.definition: The think-act-observe cycle the agent runs until it can answer.
Systems that do things: call APIs, query databases, run multi-step tasks, remember the session.

recall.question: What is the difference between RAG and agents?
recall.answer: RAG answers questions from documents; agents do things like calling APIs and running multi-step tasks.

keyTerms.definition: The reason-decide-call-read cycle the agent repeats until it can answer.
A named set of tools the agent can call, executed by a Lambda function.
The step that compiles instruction, schemas, and KB attachments after any configuration change.
A pointer at a prepared version that production traffic uses, never DRAFT.

recall.question: Why does the agent ignore a new action group?
recall.answer: prepare-agent was not run again; the agent runs the old version until then.

recall.question: How long does agent session memory last?
recall.answer: Minutes; the idle session TTL is about 600 seconds, so use a long-term memory service for weeks.

sections.title: 4.2 Action group and Lambda function contract design

keyTerms.definition: The tool definition for an existing HTTP service, describing paths, methods, and shapes.
Usually a Lambda function that Bedrock calls with a structured event.
The Lambda policy that must let the Bedrock agent invoke the action-group function.

recall.question: What breaks when the agent stops calling a tool after a redeploy?
recall.answer: The Lambda resource-based policy or IAM role changed; the policy must let the Bedrock agent invoke it.

recall.question: Why keep tool functions small and single-purpose?
recall.answer: The model only sees the schema, and long tool output wastes money and context window.

sections.title: 4.3 Multi-step task decomposition: a traced example

keyTerms.definition: What the agent splits one message into, ordered by dependency.
The X-Ray record of each step and its time, like a stack trace for an agent.

recall.question: In what order does the agent run sub-tasks?
recall.answer: By dependency; facts come before actions.

recall.question: How do you see what an agent did?
recall.answer: With the trace: X-Ray shows each step and its time.

sections.title: 4.4 Agent plus Knowledge Base plus Guardrails: the combined architecture

keyTerms.definition: Agent plus Knowledge Base plus Guardrails attached to the same agent.
The IAM role on the agent, deciding which KBs and action-group Lambdas it can use.

recall.question: What are the three parts of the exam's holy trinity?
recall.answer: The agent reasons and acts, the KB grounds it, and Guardrails keep it safe.

keyTerms.definition: The Step Functions mechanism that pauses a workflow until a human approves, even for days.
Required before the agent does sensitive actions like refunds over a limit.

recall.question: Why Step Functions instead of Lambda for approvals?
recall.answer: Lambda stops after 15 minutes; Step Functions can wait days for a task token.

recall.question: What is needed for weeks-long agent memory?
recall.answer: DynamoDB; agent sessions last only minutes.

keyTerms.definition: The invoke_agent option that returns the reasoning trace for debugging.
The memorized checklist: prepare-agent, alias version, then deeper causes.

recall.question: What is the most common agent error on the exam?
recall.answer: The agent ignoring a new action group because prepare-agent was not run again.

recall.question: How do you debug a running agent?
recall.answer: Use enableTrace on invoke_agent; the trace shows thoughts, KB queries, and tool calls.

keyTerms.definition: The agent that breaks down a task and delegates parts when a single decider is needed.
The specialist agent pattern for shared context and handoffs.
Model Context Protocol, the standard for giving agents access to tools.
The service for hosting agents from any framework with runtime, gateway, and memory.

recall.question: When do you use supervisor versus collaborator?
recall.answer: Supervisor when a single decider is needed; collaborator for shared context and handoffs.

recall.question: Why is describing inter-agent talk as action groups wrong?
recall.answer: Action groups connect agents to tools, not to agents; the exam explicitly rejects this.

keyTerms.definition: The standard design: API Gateway, Lambda, and Bedrock with memory, streaming, caching, and auth.
The stable front door that ends HTTPS, throttles, and validates requests.

recall.question: What three services form the standard serverless chatbot?
recall.answer: API Gateway, Lambda, and Bedrock.

keyTerms.definition: The API Gateway check that runs before any Lambda code, using Cognito or IAM.
The Lambda that routes requests; keep it small to control duration and cost.

recall.question: What runs before any Lambda code at the front door?
recall.answer: The authorizer on API Gateway, using Cognito for users or IAM for services.

recall.question: What goes wrong with a too-big router Lambda?
recall.answer: Duration and cost increase.

keyTerms.definition: The conversation history the model needs to stay coherent, stored per turn.
The exam's standard session store: single-digit millisecond reads with TTL expiry.
Keeping the last N turns and summarizing older ones to limit token cost per turn.

recall.question: Why is DynamoDB the standard session store?
recall.answer: Single-digit millisecond reads, TTL expiry for old sessions, and fine-grained per-user access.

recall.question: How do you trim session memory?
recall.answer: Keep the last N turns, summarize older turns, and store the summary.

keyTerms.definition: What the user feels: time to first token, not time to last token.
The streaming API where Bedrock sends tokens as server-sent events.

recall.question: Does streaming make generation faster?
recall.answer: No. It changes when the user sees the first word, not total generation time.

recall.question: How do you stream past the 29-second API Gateway limit?
recall.answer: Use WebSockets or direct SSE for long streams.

keyTerms.definition: Discounting repeated large static prefixes via a cachePoint in the Converse call.
What reduces the bill when inputs repeat; the layer before auth and model switching.

recall.question: What do you never cache?
recall.answer: Personalized or PII answers.

keyTerms.definition: The runtime configuration store for model identifiers, read by Lambda on each invocation.
The auth service for end-user sign-up, sign-in, and tiered access groups.

recall.question: What three services switch models without redeploys?
recall.answer: AppConfig holds the identifiers, Lambda routes, and API Gateway is the stable endpoint.

recall.question: Why is CloudFormation wrong for model switching?
recall.answer: Its changes are deployments, which breaks the no-code-changes requirement.

keyTerms.definition: Cost, latency, and quality: the hidden structure of every scenario question.
Converting the design into tokens to price it.

recall.question: What is every scenario question secretly about?
recall.answer: Three limits, cost, latency, and quality, plus one budget.

keyTerms.definition: The bill's parts: tokens in, tokens out, requests, and capacity.
The lever for repeated-input cost; provisioned throughput is for latency guarantees.
Service pairs the exam offers as distractors, such as caching versus provisioned throughput.

recall.question: Same long system prompt on every call: caching or provisioned throughput?
recall.answer: Prompt caching; provisioned throughput attacks latency and throttling guarantees, not repeated-input cost.

recall.question: What does each scenario verb select?
recall.answer: Unavailable in region means profiles; route by complexity means routers; guaranteed throughput means provisioned throughput.

keyTerms.definition: Input tokens times input price plus output tokens times output price.
Cost reduction is never a single answer; combine smaller model, caching, routing, compression, and eval gates.
Example prices used to show the math, not live quotes.

recall.question: What is the multi-lever rule?
recall.answer: Token costs rising 30 percent a month are never fixed by one answer; combine five levers.

recall.question: What do you start a cost estimate with?
recall.answer: Tokens, not requests; requests are only a multiplier.

keyTerms.definition: Streaming, smaller models, and provisioned throughput: what changes response time.
Retrieval quality and model size: what changes answer quality.
Keyword plus vector search combined, then merged.
A stronger model that re-scores the top chunks.

recall.question: Do temperature, top-p, and top-k control cost?
recall.answer: No. They change randomness and quality, never the invoice.

recall.question: What are the three retrieval upgrade steps?
recall.answer: Hybrid search, merge the results, then rerank with a stronger model.

keyTerms.definition: What measures quality before and after every change.
What evaluation questions punish; GenAI needs measurement, not normal-software debugging.

recall.question: Why measure quality before and after every change?
recall.answer: You cannot improve what you do not measure.

keyTerms.definition: Automatic scoring with accuracy and toxicity metrics; fast and cheap, wrong for subjective style.
An objective metric for programmatic evaluation.
What needs metrics, A/B testing, and LLM-as-a-judge; not a bigger model.

recall.question: Which evaluation fits brand voice?
recall.answer: Human evaluation or LLM-as-a-judge; programmatic scoring is wrong for subjective style.

recall.question: What is not a fairness fix?
recall.answer: A bigger model; fairness needs metrics, A/B testing, and LLM-as-a-judge.

keyTerms.definition: The metrics matched to each task type, such as faithfulness for summarization.
What you match to each task type, such as faithfulness for summarization.

recall.question: What are the summarization metrics?
recall.answer: Be faithful and do not invent facts, be complete and do not drop important information, be concise.

keyTerms.definition: Prompts with known good answers stored in S3, the base for every eval gate.
The separate model that scores outputs against a rubric prompt.
The instructions telling the judge how to score.
The judge's preference for longer answers, its own model family, and confident tone.

recall.question: What three things does a judge need?
recall.answer: Sampled outputs, a rubric prompt, and a separate judge model.

recall.question: Why calibrate LLM judges?
recall.answer: They have biases: longer answers, their own model family, confident tone.

recall.question: How much does a 500-prompt golden set cost per gate run?
recall.answer: About 10 dollars at 2 cents per judgment, cheap enough for every prompt change.

keyTerms.definition: A quality checkpoint that stops deployment when scores decrease.
Copies of real requests sent to the new version invisibly.
What A/B testing splits real users across; the winner gets promoted.

recall.question: What is the wrong monitoring tool for GenAI text quality?
recall.answer: SageMaker Model Monitor, which is for tabular ML drift, and CloudTrail, which is for audit.

recall.question: How do shadow and A/B rollouts differ?
recall.answer: Shadow sends invisible copies to the new version; A/B splits real users across two aliases.

sections.title: 8. Security hardening for a production GenAI app

keyTerms.definition: Layered controls where no single layer is the full answer.
Finding and masking personal data before the model sees it.

recall.question: What is the PII pipeline order?
recall.answer: Comprehend finds PII entities, the pipeline redacts or masks them, and Guardrails filter at the model boundary.

keyTerms.definition: What each component gets only as much of as it needs, on specific resources.
A central audited path giving each team model access without direct Bedrock calls.

recall.question: What is the exam smell in IAM?
recall.answer: One admin-style role shared by Lambda, agent, and humans; split it.

recall.question: Why is the model's built-in safety never the most correct answer?
recall.answer: Sensitive audiences need layered controls: guardrails, IAM, network, evaluation, and humans.

keyTerms.definition: Encryption for all data at rest, with customer-managed keys for compliance.
A PrivateLink interface keeping Bedrock traffic off the public internet.

recall.question: How do you keep Bedrock traffic private?
recall.answer: VPC interface endpoints for the Bedrock control plane and runtime planes.

keyTerms.definition: The audit trail: who called which API, when, and from where.
What model invocation logging to S3 or CloudWatch enables.
Which data produced an answer, via Glue Data Catalog, metadata tags, and citations.
The encryption expected on invocation log destinations holding PII.

recall.question: Trail versus Logs: which answers a bad answer?
recall.answer: Logs; Trail is for compliance like who accessed the KB, Logs is for debugging like why the agent chose that tool.

recall.question: What must a healthcare team do about invocation logs?
recall.answer: Encrypt them with KMS or disable logging, since they can contain PII.

keyTerms.definition: Guardrails categories like hate and violence, each with a severity threshold.
The control that blocks subject matter, such as medical diagnoses.
The check that an answer is supported by the retrieved document.
The input pre-filter in the layering pattern, before Guardrails on the model call.

recall.question: Prevent the model from discussing medical diagnoses: which control?
recall.answer: Denied topics; content filters cover toxicity, not topics.

recall.question: Redact SSNs: which control?
recall.answer: Sensitive information filters, not word filters.

keyTerms.definition: The service that scans S3 buckets for PII at rest and at scale.
The text service for real-time PII detection and redaction in flight.
The three PII surfaces: at rest, in flight, and at inference, one service per plane.

recall.question: Which three services protect PII in customer-service GenAI conversations?
recall.answer: Macie at rest, Comprehend in flight, and Guardrails at inference.

recall.question: Why is Rekognition wrong for chat text PII?
recall.answer: It is a vision service; Comprehend is the text answer.

keyTerms.definition: The ladder for how the answer stays factual: prompt, RAG, agents, fine-tuning.
Where every ladder starts; you must explain why you stop at that option.
What exam scenarios give you; the ladders turn them into choices.

recall.question: How do you use a ladder on a scenario?
recall.answer: Start at the top, go down until all requirements are met, then stop.

keyTerms.definition: The ladder for how the answer stays factual: prompt engineering, RAG, agents, fine-tuning.
How much more each grounding rung costs in time and money than the one before.

sections.title: 9.1 Grounding ladder: prompt engineering to RAG to agents to fine-tuning

A question giving limits and asking for the cheapest fitting design.
